object_entity.notes: Head of the Catechetical School of Alexandria; author of Protrepticus, Paedagogus, and Stromateis; synthesized Christian faith with Greek philosophy; key witness for Alexandrian baptismal theology, eucharistic practice, asceticism, and apostolic tradition.

evidence.notes: This passage from the work attests its existence and authorship.

passage.excerpt: Being baptized, we are illuminated; illuminated, we become sons; being made sons, we are perfected; being perfected, we are made immortal. This work is variously called grace, and illumination, and perfection, and washing: washing, by which we cleanse away our sins; grace, by which the penalties accruing to transgressions are remitted; and illumination, by which that holy light of salvation is beheld, that is, by which we see God clearly.
passage.notes: Baptism as illumination and new birth; the fourfold name of baptism; adoption as children of God

passage.excerpt: The blood of the Lord is twofold. For there is the blood of His flesh, by which we are redeemed from corruption; and the spiritual, that by which we are anointed. And to drink the blood of Jesus is to become partaker of the Lord's immortality; the Spirit being the energetic principle of the Word, as blood is of flesh. The mixture of water and Word is called Eucharist, renowned and glorious grace; and they who by faith partake of it are sanctified both in body and soul.
passage.notes: Eucharistic blood of Christ; real and spiritual redemption through the Eucharist; body and soul sanctified

object_entity.description: Fasting is a required Christian spiritual discipline presented as obligatory, not merely optional.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Clement instructs that frugality of diet and sobriety of living constitute the ascetic discipline of the Christian; the body is to be trained by simple food, temperance, and voluntary fasting, so that the soul may be free to pursue wisdom and prayer without the hindrance of luxury or fleshly desire.
passage.notes: Ascetic discipline; fasting and temperance for the sake of the soul; against bodily luxury

object_entity.proposition_label: Christ truly became flesh and truly suffered in the body
object_entity.description: The incarnate Christ was a genuine human being who truly was born, truly suffered, truly died, and truly rose again; not a phantom or appearance as the Docetists claimed.

context_place.notes: Major Egyptian port city; intellectual and commercial center; seat of the Catechetical School; major Christian center from the first century onward.

passage.excerpt: Let spectacles, then, and plays that are full of scurrility and of abundant mimicry, be fled from. For what base action is there that is not exhibited in the theatres? And what shameless saying is there which is not brought forward by the buffoons? And those who enjoy the evil stamp the image of it at home. And the ears are to be kept from pollution; since I think it wrong even to look on those things, much more to hear them.
passage.notes: Christians must avoid theaters, games, and public spectacles; moral contamination through entertainment

object_entity.proposition_label: Virginity and celibacy are honored as a positive Christian calling
object_entity.description: Virginity and celibacy are not merely tolerated but positively honored as a higher calling, even while marriage is defended as legitimate and good.

passage.excerpt: Paraphrase: Clement defends marriage as God-ordained and honorable for the begetting of children, citing Paul that it is better to marry than to burn; yet he honors continence as a higher calling when freely chosen for the love of God, insisting both states are legitimate and neither is to be despised.
passage.notes: Marriage defended; celibacy honored as higher calling; against both encratite rejection and licentiousness
